name: An unknown figure stays unknown through and, or, not and equality
why: The rule the rest of the arithmetic was already following and the boolean operators were not. `Compare` answers null for a comparison it cannot make, and every boolean operator used to coerce that straight back to false — so `not ((a / b) < 1)` on a record with a blank divisor answered TRUE, having quietly decided that a figure nobody could work out was below the threshold. A guard reading that would fire on every uncomputed row.

cases.why: First, the thing that is NOT unknown. A blank boolean field is FALSE, exactly as a blank number is zero. Only a figure that could not be worked out is unknown, and an empty checkbox was worked out fine.
Two blank checkboxes are equal, because both are definitely false.
Now the unknown. The balance could not be worked out, so whether it is below the threshold is unknown — this is the case every one below is built on.
Negating something nobody knows still leaves nobody knowing it. This answered TRUE before.
AND with a true: the unknown decides the answer, so the answer is unknown.
AND with a false: FALSE, definitely. This is why three-valued logic is worth having rather than refusing the whole expression — the unknown cannot change the answer, so the answer is still known.
OR with a true: TRUE, definitely, and the mirror of the case above.
OR with a false: the unknown decides it again.
Two unknowns are not equal — they are two things nobody knows. Answering TRUE here is C#'s lifted equality on `bool?`, which is two-valued logic wearing a nullable type.
And inequality against a known boolean is unknown for the same reason.
An unknown nested two deep still comes out. Nothing along the way is entitled to decide it.
But a definite answer that came THROUGH an unknown stays definite. `and false` settles it, and negating a settled false is a settled true.
